PREVENTIVE DENTISTRY FLUORIDE PROGRAM STANDARD The Board of Health shall ensure: (1) (a) That the fluoride level in the water supply of those communities where fluoride is added to the water, be monitored at least once per month. (b) That where the results of such monitoring indicate a fluoride level other than 1.2 ppm, the persons responsible for the operation of the water supply are notified of such results in order that action can be taken to bring the fluoride level to 1.2 ppm. (2) That water ‘luoridation be promoted in communities where the natural fluoride level is below 0.7 ppm. (3) That a program of fluoride supplements be promoted for children up to the age of 13 with particular emphasis on preschool children in communities where the level of fluoride in water system(s) is below 0.7 ppm. IMPLEMENTATION (1) Program Monitoring In order to indicate whether or not the Standard has been complied with, the following minimum information shall be provided, on request, to the Ministry of Health: (a) Details of the monitoring programs carried out under item (1a) of the Standard and the results thereof. (b) Evidence, satisfactory to the Ministry, that promotional campaigns as envisaged under items (2) and (3) of the Standard have been conducted. (2) Staffing The services and activities referred to in the Standard shall be carried out by public health dental staff under the direction of the Board of Health’s senior ranking public health dentist, with other staff being assigned where appropriate. (3) Program Delivery (a) The intent of item (2) of the Standard may be met through: (i) promotion of water fluoridation through such measures as the media, displays, presentations to community groups. (ii) the testing of water in non-fluoridated areas on request. (b) Under item (3) of the Standard the Fluoride
Standard may be met through: (i) promotion of water fluoridation through such measures as the media, displays, presentations to community groups. (ii) the testing of water in non-fluoridated areas on request. (b) Under item (3) of the Standard the Fluoride Supplement Program shall be carried out in accordance with accepted standards of practise. (c) The use of supplements shall be promoted in non-fluoridated areas for infants and children up to age 13 through the family physicians, dentists and other community health professionals.

Occupational Fatalities: Alberta, 1993 to 1998 An occupational fatality is the death of a worker which results from a work-related incident or exposure. Alberta Human Resources and Employment classifies occupational fatalities into three general event types: motor vehicle incidents; workplace incident; and occupational disease. Each of these three is described in more details below. Motor Vehicle Incident Motor vehicle incidents typically involve highway vehicles operating on public roads in which the fatally injured worker was either a driver or passenger. This category includes fatalities involving air plane crashes, train crashes, helicopter crashes, and so on. ‘ Fatal workplace incidents consist of cases in which the worker dies at a work site, or dies as a result of injuries sustained at a work site. It is this type of occupational fatality that Alberta Human Resources and Employment may be responsible for investigating. Occupational Disease Occupational disease fatalities consist mostly of recognized occupational disease, that is, disease known to be primarily or exclusively work-related (eg., asbestosis, black lung disease). Occupational disease are frequently diagnosed many years after the initial or crucial exposure to the toxic substance, and in such cases it is very difficult to determine when the fatal exposure occurred. The occupational disease category, then, should not be interpreted to reflect present work site hazardous conditions or exposures. pages.text: 16. The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, and more particularly the regulations under this Act, provide for common or generic names of products being displayed on the label. Regulation 14 (b) states: "The following information shall be shown on the principal display panel:...the identity of the prepackaged product in terms of its common or generic name or in terms of its function." We have here the essence of one of the key terms of the OSHA Proposed Draft Standard, although an alternative to the common or generic name is provided, viz., identification of the product "in terms of its function." The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act, how- ever, is not intended to provide protection to workers, but only to consumers. This is made clear in Regulation 3(1): "Prepackaged products that are produced or manufactured for commercial or industrial enterprises or institutions for use by such enterprises or institutions without being sold by them as prepackaged products to other consumers are exempt from all the provisions of the Act." Thus if we wish to find Canadian law which protects the citizen as worker to the same extent as the citizen as consumer is protected, . shall have to look elsewhere for it. The Hazardous Products Act, as itsname applies, is intended to apply to known hazardous products only. Moreover, being administered by Consumer and Corporate Affairs, it is intended to protect the consumer and not the worker. A brief overview of this Act reveals some interesting character- istics. In this Act, a “hazardous product" is one which is included on one of two lists. Products on the first list, Part I of the Schedule, are dis- allowed. These include such products as jequirity beans; children's furniture finished with lead paint; toys containing carbon tetrachloride, methyl alcohol, petroleum distillates, benzene, etc.

In Metropolitan Toronto, for example, only two hospitals support a full-time occupational medical director: Wellesley Hospital/Princess Margaret Hospital, and The Toronto Hospital/Toronto General and Western Divisions. In addition to the lay assumption that hospitals are inherently healthful places in which to work, there are other factors that have inhibited the development of health and safety programs. The ‘treatment-of- disease’ orientation has tended to pre-—empt competing interests in preventive medicine and health maintenance, while preoccupation with the patient’s care and environment took precedence over the people providing such care. Professional and technological staff were assumed to be self- sufficient in the management of their own oc- cupational health, while support staff often had little guidance at all. The availability of spontaneous informal medical opinion and/or treatment often aborted the reporting process of work-related health concerns and hindered the need for a more or- ganized response. Finally, hospital funding, whether from government, direct patient accounts or en—- dowments, has always been committed to direct patient care along with the other twin priorities of teaching and research. Only during the last decade have funds been more willingly allocated to employee occupational health and the monitoring of environmental biohazards. In Ontario, hospital unions formerly pursued monetary and benefit considerations. However, the occupational health and safety legislation has established a link between hospitals and the Ministry of Labour, and has caused unions to focus on occupational health issues in hospitals. pages.text: Chapter 4 Discussion 4.1 Limitations of the study: 4.1.1 Scope This review did not address all the aspects of patients occupying an acute care bed when they could have been cared for more appropriately in another setting. This study looked at the barriers to transition - what delays or barriers prevented timely discharge from acute care? Other issues such as inappropriate admission were not specifically considered. In planning this review, the Team was aware that utilization management reporting in a format that allowed comparison was non-existent in the province. There was no one standardized tool in use that all hospital administrators, physicians, nurses or discharge planners were familiar with and using on a regular basis. Therefore, it is acknowledged that the results are affected by a learning curve. It has been shown that when institutions first employ utilization management techniques and tools, there tends to be under reporting at first while the participants learn to recognize the nuances of the new system. Many of the participants in this study were not familiar with utilization review tools and techniques. 4.1.2 Use of a new survey instrument In order to have a consistent reporting tool for use province-wide, the Team developed a new survey instrument. Will vaccination eradicate brucellosis? No. Vaccination plays a useful role in controlling the spread of the disease. In the early stages of brucel- losis control in Canada, vaccination reduced the level of infection to a point where it was possible to proceed with a test-and-slaughter program to eradicate the disease and establish areas free from brucellosis. As we are now reaching the final stages of brucellosis eradication, there is less need for a vaccination program. Should an owner continue a vaccination program in his herd? The Health of Animals Branch considers that it is no longer necessary to carry out a vaccination program except where the incidence of brucellosis in a herd or an area warrants it. The Health of Animals Branch conducts two screen- ing programs: Brucellosis Milk Ring Tests — Milk and cream sam- ples collected at dairies and creameries are tested for brucellosis. At the same time, the anti-smoking lobby has grown increasingly vocal about the social costs of smoking and of tolerating the habit in public places. These groups are pressuring federal and provincial governments to legislate against tobacco advertising and smoking in the workplace, to declare tobacco a hazardous substance and to assist tobacco farmers to find alternative crops or alternative employment. The tobacco farmers, however, want a national marketing board to help maintain prices and to find new markets in Canada and abroad. Tobacco manufacturers are buying less tobacco from farmers because of declining domestic sales of cigarettes, which they blame mainly on rising government taxes, and increased foreign competition for the export market. Rationalization and diversification have maintained profits for some tobacco manufacturers, but communities dependent on tobacco growing are suffering financially because they cannot sell their crops. Health and Welfare Canada has initiated anti-smoking campaigns aimed at youth and has expressed increased concern about the rising health costs associated with the preventable illnesses that result from tobacco use. While placing voluntary restrictions on tobacco advertising, however, the federal government has continued to subsidize the tobacco farmers.

While the shift in public opinion supporting non- smoking has been evident since about 1980, stronger measures have recently been implemented in order to protect non-smckers from smoke, to encourage smokers to quit, and to encourage non-smokers to remain smoke-free. Two federal government policies have had an impact on smokers and on tobacco companies. These are tobacco taxation and tobacco advertising controls. Smokers now pay close to $5.00 for a pack of 20 cigarettes. Research that connects tobacco to disease, along with expressed public opinion against smoking, has encouraged legislators to tax tobacco extensively. There is some evidence that high tobacco prices encourage people to stop smoking. While taxation targets the consumer, the 1989 Tobacco Advertising Controls Products Control Act targets tobacco advertising and = its association with the “good life.” The Act phases out advertising and places increased restrictions on the promotion of cigarettes and tobacco. pages.text: CANADA LIBRARY OF PARLIAMENT BIBLIOTHEQUE DU PARLEMENT TOBACCO SMOKING* ISSUE DEFINITION Over the past two or three decades, North America has witnessed a revolution in attitudes towards tobacco smoking. What was once considered a normal habit has become increasingly socially unacceptable. An ever-growing number of non-smokers are much less tolerant of smoking, and anti-smoking activists have become very vocal in their opposition to the habit. Governments and other organizations are more receptive to lobbying efforts and are introducing bans and restrictions on smoking. Since the 1960s, research has documented the health hazards of tobacco smoking. Originally, the emphasis was on the danger to the smoker, but it has become clear in recent years that non-smokers are also at risk from inhaling second-hand or "“sidestream" smoke. While most experts and governments accept the scientific and medical evidence of the dangers of tobacco smoke, changes do not come easily. Both the Surgeon General in the United States and the Royal Society of Canada have concluded that tobacco is a highly addictive~-product and many smokers find it difficult, if not impossible, to stop smoking, even if they want to. pages.text: 2012 Ontario Budget Tobacco Enforcement Tobacco use continues to be the leading cause of preventable disease and premature death in Ontario. The government’s Smoke-Free Ontario Strategy has made the province a leader in tobacco control. Ontario remains committed to reducing smoking among youth and other vulnerable persons, and to achieving the lowest smoking rate in Canada. As part of this commitment, the government intends to take the necessary steps to increase fines on those convicted of selling tobacco to youth and to impose stronger sanctions for repeat offenders of Ontario’s tobacco- related laws. These sanctions would include prohibiting a retailer from selling tobacco products or lottery tickets and would be implemented by the fall. The availability of cheap, illegal tobacco makes it easier for non-smokers, especially youth, to start smoking, and removes an incentive for smokers to quit, undermining the government’s policies to reduce smoking. The government will work with key partners to further educate the public about health and social problems associated with tobacco and will undertake research to help measure the impact of its tobacco strategies on smoking levels in the province. Ontario has also committed to doubling enforcement efforts to address the supply of cheap, illegal tobacco. As part of this commitment, the government will focus on the implementation of additional regulatory, enforcement and other provisions in Bill 186, which was enacted in 2011. 258
